Ross et al. [20] showed that constraining models to produce
“right” explanations during training can improve generaliza￾tion.
Despite these advances, three structural limitations persist.
First, existing perturbation studies rarely incorporate matched
anatomical controls: they test whether a region matters, but
not whether disease-specific regions matter more than adjacent
control regions. This is the distinction between sensitivity and
specificity in explanation evaluation. Second, the perturbation
operator is rarely treated as an auditable variable—zero￾masking is the default, and its artifacts are seldom quantified.
Third, explanation conclusions are typically validated only
within the training distribution; Adebayo et al. [8] showed
that saliency maps can fail basic sanity checks under input
transformations, but the broader question of whether explana￾tion claims survive dataset shift remains underexamined [4],
[9].
C. Cross-Dataset Transfer and Generalization
The two largest public 12-lead ECG datasets—PTB-XL [21]
(21,837 records, cardiologist-validated labels) and CODE-15%
[22] (345,779 exams, automated labels)—differ fundamentally
in their label sources. This asymmetry creates a natural testbed
for transfer stability: models trained on automated labels may
learn to replicate the labeling logic rather than physician-level
diagnostic features. Cross-dataset validation remains underuti￾lized in ECG deep learning. Soltanieh et al. [23] addressed
out-of-distribution generalization for self-supervised ECG rep￾resentations. Frank et al. [24] reported substantial performance
drops for myocardial ischemia detection across six public ECG
databases. At foundation-model scale, ECGFounder [25] and
recent benchmarking efforts [26] confirm that cross-domain
generalization remains challenging even for large pre-trained
models.
The consistent picture is that external validation is widely
recommended but rarely executed, and even less often applied
to explanation claims. Our study addresses this gap by treat￾ing frozen-weight transfer from CODE-15% to cardiologist￾validated PTB-XL fold 10 as a simultaneous check on both
prediction quality and evidence-use stability.
D. Clinical ECG Knowledge and Model Auditing
Clinical ECG interpretation relies on well-defined phys￾iological features: PR interval for AV conduction timing,
QRS duration and morphology for ventricular conduction,
RR interval regularity for rhythm classification, and P-wave
morphology for atrial activity [11]. These features define
distinct, auditable evidence units with well-characterized sig￾nal structure. Recent studies have tested whether deep ECG
models learn clinically meaningful features: Hempel et al. [27]
reported that 96.0% of high-confidence 1AVB predictions had
PR>200ms; Riberg et al. [28] found that RR interval fea￾tures dominated for bradycardia while morphological features
showed weaker correlation; Hammer et al. [29] introduced an
architecture separating rhythm and morphology processing. A
systematic review by Ayano et al. [30] confirmed increasing
focus on clinical parameters.
However, existing studies confirm that models attend to
clinically relevant features but do not test whether disease￾specific signal regions dominate over anatomically adjacent
controls, or whether such pathway specificity survives dataset
shift. Demonstrating feature relevance is not the same as
demonstrating feature specificity. Our framework addresses
this gap by transforming clinical pathway knowledge into
testable, falsifiable audit criteria with matched controls and
external transfer.
III. METHODS
A. Audit Framework Overview
The audit framework has four general components: domain￾defined target evidence units, matched controls, operator￾specified perturbation, and external transfer testing. Fig. 1
summarizes the workflow instantiated in 12-lead ECG clas￾sification:
1) Domain-knowledge-defined evidence panel: For each
diagnosis, target evidence units and matched controls
are pre-specified from established domain knowledge.
In our ECG instantiation, five diagnoses covering three
structurally distinct evidence forms—interval-localized
timing (1AVB), QRS morphology (CRBBB, CLBBB),
and distributed rate/rhythm (SBRAD, AFIB)—serve as
a case-study panel (Section III-C).
2) Matched-control perturbation: The same perturbation
operator is applied to both the target evidence unit
and each matched control. An evidence-use claim re￾quires the target perturbation to be more disruptive than
its strongest matched control. Perturbation classes are
matched to evidence-unit structure: local windows for
temporally localized features, global transformations for
distributed statistical properties (Section III-D).
3) Audit metrics and evidence tiers: The Anatomical
Specificity Score (ASS) quantifies whether the target
perturbation dominates all matched controls. Per-model
evidence tiers constrain what can be claimed under the
primary operator (Section III-E).
4) External transfer testing: Frozen-weight transfer to an
independent dataset tests whether evidence-use conclu￾sions survive dataset shift (Section III-B).
The framework is model-agnostic: the same evidence units,
matched-control comparisons, and evaluation metrics apply to
any classifier accepting the same input modality. We demon￾strate this across three raw-signal architectures (Section III-F),
with XGBoost feature-space baselines providing contextual
representation-level evidence. The five diagnoses are a case￾study panel covering three structurally distinct evidence forms,
not an exhaustive clinical survey.

Internal cohort — CODE-15%. Brazilian 12-lead ECG
dataset: 345,779 exams (400Hz, 10 s) from 233,770 patients
[22]. Labels were derived from an automated ECG interpre￾tation system. Patient-level split: 60% train (207,232), 20%
validation (69,045), 20% test (69,520), random seed 42.

C. ECG Instantiation: Domain-Knowledge-Defined Evidence
Panel
The audit framework requires that target evidence units and
matched controls be specified a priori from domain knowledge.
In our ECG instantiation, we construct a compact, literature￾guided panel covering five diagnoses. For each disease we
pre-specify (i) the expected positive evidence unit, (ii) matched
control regions that should produce smaller effects, and (iii)
any ambiguous evidence unit treated as an exploratory hypoth￾esis. Table I summarises the full panel including perturbation
class and target window definitions.
Domain-knowledge grounding. Each target and control
pairing is grounded in established ECG diagnostic criteria [11].
The target maps to the clinically accepted diagnostic feature
(PR prolongation for 1AVB, QRS widening for BBB, low
ventricular rate for SBRAD, absent P-waves for AFIB). Each
matched control is anatomically adjacent but physiologically
distinct (e.g., ST segment vs. PR-target window, QRS complex
vs. atrial window), so that the control probes a plausible
alternative signal channel rather than a trivially irrelevant
region. This design operationalizes the distinction between
perturbation sensitivity (does the target region matter?) and
anatomical specificity (does it matter more than matched
controls?).
D. Perturbation Design
The perturbation class should match the structure of the
domain evidence unit. We apply two classes of signal interven￾tion: Class I (local window) for features localized to a specific
ECG interval, and Class II (global transformation) for fea￾tures distributed across the recording. This taxonomy ensures
each disease is tested via the intervention class appropriate to
its clinical definition. All perturbations share matched-subset
construction (equal-sized positive/negative cohorts, random
seed 42) and uncertainty quantification (patient-level bootstrap,
n = 1, 000 iterations).
1) Perturbation Operator and Protocol: For all local￾window perturbations, a predefined temporal window is cen￾tered relative to each detected R-peak and applied across all 12
leads. The primary perturbation operator is linear interpolation:
the signal segment within the window is replaced by a straight
line between boundary values, preserving local waveform
continuity (Fig. 2). We selected linear interpolation via a
predefined four-operator comparison battery (Supplementary
Material), which demonstrated that zero-masking—the most
common occlusion method—creates hard-boundary artifacts
that systematically inflate control-region disruption and can
reverse evidence-use conclusions. All evidence-use conclu￾sions are conditional on this operator choice. Random-window
controls use 5 random placements per exam averaged via logit
averaging.
2) Class I: Local Window Perturbation: For evidence units
localized to a specific interval, the perturbation window is
defined relative to each R-peak: PR-target window (120 ms,
[R−200 ms, R−80 ms)) for 1AVB; QRS complex (160 ms,
centered at R-peak) for CRBBB and CLBBB; atrial win￾dow ([R−200 ms, R−40 ms]) for AFIB. Matched controls
are anatomically adjacent windows targeting physiologically
distinct structures. For 1AVB, the PR-target and QRS-control
windows are adjacent but non-overlapping—they meet at
R−80 ms, ensuring no sample point belongs to both windows.
The same operator is applied to both target and controls.
Samples with fewer than 3 detectable R-peaks are excluded.
3) Class II: Global Signal Transformation: When the ev￾idence unit is a statistical property of the entire recording,
local window perturbation is inappropriate. Instead, the signal
is time-warped to selectively disrupt the target property while
preserving local beat morphology (Supplementary Fig. 5).
SBRAD targets low ventricular rate via rate normalization
(time-warp to 75 bpm). Because rate is a global property, the
target perturbation is global; matched controls use local linear
interpolation on QRS, ST, and random non-QRS windows—
this hybrid design tests whether rate information specifically
exceeds morphology-based alternatives.
AFIB spans both classes: RR irregularity (global) is tested
via RR regularization with beat-order permutation as func￾tional control; atrial activity (local) is tested via Class I atrial￾window perturbation. This dual-class design maps to the two
clinical hallmarks of AFIB.

choice can determine audit conclusions.
Conclusion: Discrimination, target sensitivity, and domain￾evidence concordance measure distinct properties: in this ECG
case study, high AUROC did not guarantee knowledge-aligned ev￾idence use, and target-only perturbation would have misclassified
several model-disease pairs as Pathway-supported. Matched con￾trols, operator comparison, and frozen-weight external validation
address complementary failure modes in evidence-use auditing:
non-specific target sensitivity, operator-induced artifacts, and
dataset-specific explanations. The framework is not ECG-specific
in principle, but its extension to other domains requires a
priori specification of domain-relevant evidence units, plausible
matched controls, and appropriate perturbation operators.
Index Terms—domain-evidence concordance, knowledge￾aligned evidence use, matched-control perturbation audit, op￾erator comparison, cross-dataset transfer, evidence tiers, ECG
classification
I. INTRODUCTION
Deep learning classifiers now achieve high discrimination
across a wide range of biomedical tasks, from ECG inter￾pretation [1]–[3] to radiological imaging and physiological
monitoring. However, high discrimination does not establish
that a model relies on evidence consistent with established
diagnostic criteria, or that such reliance persists under dataset
shift. Models can exploit statistically correlated but mechanis￾tically irrelevant shortcuts—dataset-specific artifacts, acquisi￾tion confounds, or proxy features that happen to covary with
the target label within the training distribution [4], [5]. When
such models are deployed in new settings, these shortcuts may
vanish, and the performance measured by benchmark metrics
may not generalize.
Existing explanation and interpretability methods address
part of this problem but leave three structural gaps. First, most
perturbation-based and attribution-based methods test whether
an input region matters, not whether disease-specific regions
matter more than matched controls [6], [7]. This conflates
perturbation sensitivity (a region is important) with anatomical
specificity (a disease-relevant region dominates over matched
alternatives)—a distinction with direct consequences for clini￾cal trustworthiness. Second, the perturbation operator itself is
rarely treated as an auditable methodological variable: the most
common choice, zero-masking, introduces hard-boundary ar￾tifacts whose influence on explanation conclusions is seldom
quantified [8]. Third, explanation conclusions are almost never
validated under external dataset shift; an explanation conclu￾sion that holds within the training distribution may not survive
transfer to an independent dataset with different population
characteristics, acquisition protocols, or label sources [9],
[10]. These three gaps—the absence of matched controls,
unexamined operator dependence, and the lack of external
transfer testing—mean that standard explanation workflows
can produce conclusions that are internally plausible but
externally fragile.
We address these gaps with a matched-control perturbation
audit framework built on four design principles: (1) evi￾dence units are pre-specified from domain knowledge; (2) an
evidence-use claim requires the target perturbation to exceed
its strongest matched control; (3) the perturbation operator
is selected through a predefined comparison battery; and (4)
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 2 / 22>

IEEE JOURNAL OF BIOMEDICAL AND HEALTH INFORMATICS, VOL. XX, NO. XX, MONTH 2025 2
all conclusions are re-tested under frozen-weight transfer to
an independent dataset. The framework is model-agnostic:
the same perturbation windows, matched-control comparisons,
and evaluation metrics apply to any classifier accepting the
same input modality.
We instantiate this framework in 12-lead ECG classifi￾cation, where standard diagnostic criteria define temporally
and physiologically grounded evidence units—including PR￾interval timing, QRS duration and morphology, ventricular
rate, and atrial activity [11]—against which matched con￾trols can be specified a priori. We construct a five-disease
audit panel whose diagnoses were selected to cover three
structurally distinct ECG evidence forms: interval-localized
timing (first-degree AV block, 1AVB), QRS-localized mor￾phology (complete right and left bundle branch block,
CRBBB/CLBBB), and distributed rate/rhythm statistics (sinus
bradycardia, SBRAD; atrial fibrillation, AFIB). This structural
diversity requires two perturbation classes—local window and
global transformation—and ensures the audit is not limited to
a single evidence type. For each disease, target regions and
anatomically matched controls are grounded in standard ECG
interpretation rules, and perturbation classes are matched to
evidence-unit structure.
We apply the matched-control waveform audit across
three raw-signal architectures: ResNet, SE-ResNet, and a
lightweight Transformer, to assess whether evidence-use con￾clusions are architecture-dependent or architecture-invariant.
Feature-space XGBoost baselines (using simple summary
features and timing-enriched Clinical-MVP features) provide
representation-level context for discrimination, but operate
on precomputed features rather than raw waveforms and are
therefore outside the scope of the waveform perturbation audit.
The protocol is evaluated internally on CODE-15% (345,779
exams, patient-level split) and externally on PTB-XL fold 10
(cardiologist-validated labels).
Our primary contributions are fivefold:
1) Matched controls prevent false evidence-specificity
claims. Single-region PR perturbation produces
∆AUROC=−0.226 and would, without controls,
suggest Pathway-supported for 1AVB. QRS-matched
perturbation is more disruptive (−0.351), reversing
this conclusion across all architectures and datasets.
This establishes matched controls as a required
methodological safeguard.
2) Operator choice determines audit verdicts. The same
model-disease pair yields opposite conclusions under
different operators: AFIB appears Pathway-supported
under zero-masking but Not supported under linear
interpolation; CRBBB appears transfer-unstable under
zero-masking but Pathway-supported under linear in￾terpolation. Operator comparison should be a required
component of perturbation auditing.
3) Deep ECG models robustly encode QRS morphology
but not PR-timing, rate, or atrial activity. Only
CRBBB and CLBBB reach Pathway-supported across
all architectures and datasets. 1AVB, AFIB, and SBRAD
fail specificity despite matching or exceeding clinical de￾tection rates—a dissociation between clinical diagnostic
criteria and model evidence use.
4) Evidence-use stability is diagnosis-specific. Cross￾dataset frozen-weight transfer shows QRS-morphology
evidence is invariant (CDDC=1.0, all models), while
PR-timing and atrial-activity evidence are dataset￾dependent. This identifies which ECG predictions may
transfer reliably across populations and which may not.
5) Discrimination does not certify evidence alignment.
Across 15 model-disease pairs with uniformly high
AUROC (>0.93 after frozen transfer), only 6 reach
Pathway-supported. Standard benchmarks alone are in￾sufficient to evaluate whether models use clinically
meaningful features.
II. RELATED WORK
A. Deep Learning Evaluation Beyond Discrimination
The standard evaluation framework for biomedical deep
learning emphasizes discrimination metrics—AUROC, F1,
sensitivity, specificity—on held-out test splits. This tradition
has produced strong benchmark results across ECG classifica￾tion [1], [2], [12], radiology, and pathology. However, a grow￾ing body of work demonstrates that high discrimination can
coexist with reliance on clinically irrelevant features. DeGrave
et al. [5] showed that deep learning models for radiographic
COVID-19 detection exploited shortcut features rather than
meaningful pathology. Geirhos et al. [4] documented that
ImageNet-trained CNNs rely on texture rather than shape,
violating human perceptual strategies. In ECG specifically,
Ong Ly et al. [10] demonstrated that hidden data acquisition
biases can inflate model performance by up to 20%, with
AUROC dropping from 0.90 to 0.70 under external validation.
These findings motivate an evaluation axis orthogonal to
discrimination: does the model use evidence that aligns with
domain knowledge, and does that alignment survive dataset
shift?
B. Explanation and Perturbation-Based Audits
Post-hoc explanation methods—saliency maps, occlusion￾based sensitivity, guided backpropagation, integrated
gradients—have been systematically evaluated on ECG
tasks. Storas et al. [6] compared nine gradient-based methods ˚
and found no single method works best across measurement
tasks. Suh et al. [7] evaluated eleven attribution methods
and reported that Guided Grad-CAM best aligned with
cardiologists’ assessment. Plagwitz et al. [13] found that
explanation reliability varies substantially across attribution
methods and disease categories. Al-Zaiti et al. [14] reported
that clinically deployed saliency maps for occlusion MI
detection were rated only slightly clinically relevant by
practicing clinicians.
Perturbation-based evaluation provides a more direct test of
feature dependence. Wagner et al. [15] proposed a structured
XAI framework for ECG combining occlusion-based sanity
checks with concept-based analysis. Bender et al. [16] demon￾strated that ResNet features align with clinical diagnostic cri￾teria. Recent work has applied wave masking, reconstruction￾based perturbation, and Shapley-value-based ablation [17]–
[19] to quantify localized feature importance. Beyond ECG,
<PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 3 / 22>

IEEE JOURNAL OF BIOMEDICAL AND HEALTH INFORMATICS, VOL. XX, NO. XX, MONTH 2025 3
Ross et al. [20] showed that constraining models to produce
“right” explanations during training can improve generaliza￾tion.
Despite these advances, three structural limitations persist.
First, existing perturbation studies rarely incorporate matched
anatomical controls: they test whether a region matters, but
not whether disease-specific regions matter more than adjacent
control regions. This is the distinction between sensitivity and
specificity in explanation evaluation. Second, the perturbation
operator is rarely treated as an auditable variable—zero￾masking is the default, and its artifacts are seldom quantified.
Third, explanation conclusions are typically validated only
within the training distribution; Adebayo et al. [8] showed
that saliency maps can fail basic sanity checks under input
transformations, but the broader question of whether explana￾tion claims survive dataset shift remains underexamined [4],
[9].
C. Cross-Dataset Transfer and Generalization
The two largest public 12-lead ECG datasets—PTB-XL [21]
(21,837 records, cardiologist-validated labels) and CODE-15%
[22] (345,779 exams, automated labels)—differ fundamentally
in their label sources. This asymmetry creates a natural testbed
for transfer stability: models trained on automated labels may
learn to replicate the labeling logic rather than physician-level
diagnostic features. Cross-dataset validation remains underuti￾lized in ECG deep learning. Soltanieh et al. [23] addressed
out-of-distribution generalization for self-supervised ECG rep￾resentations. Frank et al. [24] reported substantial performance
drops for myocardial ischemia detection across six public ECG
databases. At foundation-model scale, ECGFounder [25] and
recent benchmarking efforts [26] confirm that cross-domain
generalization remains challenging even for large pre-trained
models.
The consistent picture is that external validation is widely
recommended but rarely executed, and even less often applied
to explanation claims. Our study addresses this gap by treat￾ing frozen-weight transfer from CODE-15% to cardiologist￾validated PTB-XL fold 10 as a simultaneous check on both
prediction quality and evidence-use stability.
D. Clinical ECG Knowledge and Model Auditing
Clinical ECG interpretation relies on well-defined phys￾iological features: PR interval for AV conduction timing,
QRS duration and morphology for ventricular conduction,
RR interval regularity for rhythm classification, and P-wave
morphology for atrial activity [11]. These features define
distinct, auditable evidence units with well-characterized sig￾nal structure. Recent studies have tested whether deep ECG
models learn clinically meaningful features: Hempel et al. [27]
reported that 96.0% of high-confidence 1AVB predictions had
PR>200ms; Riberg et al. [28] found that RR interval fea￾tures dominated for bradycardia while morphological features
showed weaker correlation; Hammer et al. [29] introduced an
architecture separating rhythm and morphology processing. A
systematic review by Ayano et al. [30] confirmed increasing
focus on clinical parameters.
However, existing studies confirm that models attend to
clinically relevant features but do not test whether disease￾specific signal regions dominate over anatomically adjacent
controls, or whether such pathway specificity survives dataset
shift. Demonstrating feature relevance is not the same as
demonstrating feature specificity. Our framework addresses
this gap by transforming clinical pathway knowledge into
testable, falsifiable audit criteria with matched controls and
external transfer.
III. METHODS
A. Audit Framework Overview
The audit framework has four general components: domain￾defined target evidence units, matched controls, operator￾specified perturbation, and external transfer testing. Fig. 1
summarizes the workflow instantiated in 12-lead ECG clas￾sification:
1) Domain-knowledge-defined evidence panel: For each
diagnosis, target evidence units and matched controls
are pre-specified from established domain knowledge.
In our ECG instantiation, five diagnoses covering three
structurally distinct evidence forms—interval-localized
timing (1AVB), QRS morphology (CRBBB, CLBBB),
and distributed rate/rhythm (SBRAD, AFIB)—serve as
a case-study panel (Section III-C).
2) Matched-control perturbation: The same perturbation
operator is applied to both the target evidence unit
and each matched control. An evidence-use claim re￾quires the target perturbation to be more disruptive than
its strongest matched control. Perturbation classes are
matched to evidence-unit structure: local windows for
temporally localized features, global transformations for
distributed statistical properties (Section III-D).
3) Audit metrics and evidence tiers: The Anatomical
Specificity Score (ASS) quantifies whether the target
perturbation dominates all matched controls. Per-model
evidence tiers constrain what can be claimed under the
primary operator (Section III-E).
4) External transfer testing: Frozen-weight transfer to an
independent dataset tests whether evidence-use conclu￾sions survive dataset shift (Section III-B).
The framework is model-agnostic: the same evidence units,
matched-control comparisons, and evaluation metrics apply to
any classifier accepting the same input modality. We demon￾strate this across three raw-signal architectures (Section III-F),
with XGBoost feature-space baselines providing contextual
representation-level evidence. The five diagnoses are a case￾study panel covering three structurally distinct evidence forms,
not an exhaustive clinical survey.
B. Datasets and External Validation Setting
Internal cohort — CODE-15%. Brazilian 12-lead ECG
dataset: 345,779 exams (400Hz, 10 s) from 233,770 patients
[22]. Labels were derived from an automated ECG interpre￾tation system. Patient-level split: 60% train (207,232), 20%
validation (69,045), 20% test (69,520), random seed 42.

Label circularity risk. Because CODE-15% labels are au￾tomated rather than physician-adjudicated, models trained on
them may learn to replicate the automated labeling logic
instead of physician-level diagnostic mechanisms. The circu￾larity risk is highest for 1AVB and SBRAD, where automated
rules closely mirror the target features (PR>200 ms and HR￾based thresholds, respectively), moderate for CRBBB/CLBBB
and AFIB, where QRS morphology and atrial activity criteria
are less directly encoded. Internal CODE findings should
therefore be interpreted as evidence about model behavior
relative to the automated-label system. External validation on
cardiologist-validated labels provides the primary credibility
buffer.
External cohort — PTB-XL. German 12-lead ECG
dataset: 21,837 records from 18,885 patients at 500 Hz [21].
We use official patient-level folds: folds 1–8 for reference, fold
9 (n = 2, 183) for threshold retuning, and fold 10 (n = 2, 198)
for testing. Fold 10 labels were validated by cardiologists
and serve as the primary external credibility set. SCP-ECG
diagnostic codes were mapped to the five target diseases using
strict primary code matching.
Transfer and evaluation protocol. CODE-trained models
are applied to PTB-XL without fine-tuning (frozen weights).
PTB-XL signals are downsampled from 500 Hz to 400 Hz
via Fourier resampling, trimmed/padded to 4,096 samples,
and z-score normalized per lead with lead order matching
CODE-15%. We report three transfer levels: (1) strict frozen—
CODE validation thresholds applied directly to fold 10; (2)
calibrated—thresholds retuned on fold 9; (3) oracle upper
bound—optimal thresholds on fold 10. AUROC is threshold￾invariant and serves as the primary frozen-generalization met￾ric.
C. ECG Instantiation: Domain-Knowledge-Defined Evidence
Panel
The audit framework requires that target evidence units and
matched controls be specified a priori from domain knowledge.
In our ECG instantiation, we construct a compact, literature￾guided panel covering five diagnoses. For each disease we
pre-specify (i) the expected positive evidence unit, (ii) matched
control regions that should produce smaller effects, and (iii)
any ambiguous evidence unit treated as an exploratory hypoth￾esis. Table I summarises the full panel including perturbation
class and target window definitions.
Domain-knowledge grounding. Each target and control
pairing is grounded in established ECG diagnostic criteria [11].
The target maps to the clinically accepted diagnostic feature
(PR prolongation for 1AVB, QRS widening for BBB, low
ventricular rate for SBRAD, absent P-waves for AFIB). Each
matched control is anatomically adjacent but physiologically
distinct (e.g., ST segment vs. PR-target window, QRS complex
vs. atrial window), so that the control probes a plausible
alternative signal channel rather than a trivially irrelevant
region. This design operationalizes the distinction between
perturbation sensitivity (does the target region matter?) and
anatomical specificity (does it matter more than matched
controls?).
D. Perturbation Design
The perturbation class should match the structure of the
domain evidence unit. We apply two classes of signal interven￾tion: Class I (local window) for features localized to a specific
ECG interval, and Class II (global transformation) for fea￾tures distributed across the recording. This taxonomy ensures
each disease is tested via the intervention class appropriate to
its clinical definition. All perturbations share matched-subset
construction (equal-sized positive/negative cohorts, random
seed 42) and uncertainty quantification (patient-level bootstrap,
n = 1, 000 iterations).
1) Perturbation Operator and Protocol: For all local￾window perturbations, a predefined temporal window is cen￾tered relative to each detected R-peak and applied across all 12
leads. The primary perturbation operator is linear interpolation:
the signal segment within the window is replaced by a straight
line between boundary values, preserving local waveform
continuity (Fig. 2). We selected linear interpolation via a
predefined four-operator comparison battery (Supplementary
Material), which demonstrated that zero-masking—the most
common occlusion method—creates hard-boundary artifacts
that systematically inflate control-region disruption and can
reverse evidence-use conclusions. All evidence-use conclu￾sions are conditional on this operator choice. Random-window
controls use 5 random placements per exam averaged via logit
averaging.
2) Class I: Local Window Perturbation: For evidence units
localized to a specific interval, the perturbation window is
defined relative to each R-peak: PR-target window (120 ms,
[R−200 ms, R−80 ms)) for 1AVB; QRS complex (160 ms,
centered at R-peak) for CRBBB and CLBBB; atrial win￾dow ([R−200 ms, R−40 ms]) for AFIB. Matched controls
are anatomically adjacent windows targeting physiologically
distinct structures. For 1AVB, the PR-target and QRS-control
windows are adjacent but non-overlapping—they meet at
R−80 ms, ensuring no sample point belongs to both windows.
The same operator is applied to both target and controls.
Samples with fewer than 3 detectable R-peaks are excluded.
3) Class II: Global Signal Transformation: When the ev￾idence unit is a statistical property of the entire recording,
local window perturbation is inappropriate. Instead, the signal
is time-warped to selectively disrupt the target property while
preserving local beat morphology (Supplementary Fig. 5).
SBRAD targets low ventricular rate via rate normalization
(time-warp to 75 bpm). Because rate is a global property, the
target perturbation is global; matched controls use local linear
interpolation on QRS, ST, and random non-QRS windows—
this hybrid design tests whether rate information specifically
exceeds morphology-based alternatives.
AFIB spans both classes: RR irregularity (global) is tested
via RR regularization with beat-order permutation as func￾tional control; atrial activity (local) is tested via Class I atrial￾window perturbation. This dual-class design maps to the two
clinical hallmarks of AFIB.
The full perturbation taxonomy is given in Table I. Sample
sizes for perturbation experiments per disease: 1AVB n =
2, 284; CRBBB n = 3, 184; CLBBB n = 2, 126; SBRAD
n = 1, 190; AFIB n = 1, 256 (positives, with equal number

D. Operator Selection Determines Audit Conclusions
The predefined operator-comparison battery demonstrates
that perturbation operator choice can determine audit conclu￾sions. The same model-disease pair can yield opposite verdicts
under different operators (Section V-E, Type 4), establishing
operator comparison as a methodological requirement rather
than a sensitivity check.
This finding has direct implications for the broader
perturbation-audit literature. Zero-masking remains the most
common occlusion method in ECG and medical imaging per￾turbation studies, yet our results show it can reverse specificity
conclusions. We recommend that future perturbation-based
audit studies: (1) compare at least two operators with different
artifact profiles; (2) prespecify the primary operator before
seeing results; and (3) report operator-comparison results
alongside primary-operator conclusions. Linear interpolation
is not claimed to be universally optimal, but its continuity￾preserving property eliminates a known artifact class that zero￾masking introduces.
E. Interpreting Audit Verdicts: Why Pathways Are Supported,
Limited, or Not Supported
The audit assigns each (architecture, disease) pair to one
of three evidence tiers. These verdicts do not map directly to
judgments of model correctness or clinical reasoning ability.
We interpret each tier’s meaning and, for Not-supported ver￾dicts, disentangle the distinct mechanisms that can produce a
negative ASS.
Pathway-supported indicates that, under the pre-specified
target and control windows, the primary perturbation op￾erator, and external transfer validation, the target evidence
unit dominates all matched anatomical controls. It does not
certify that the model “reasons like a clinician” or that the
mechanism is physiologically causal (Section V-G). In this
study, CRBBB and CLBBB achieve Pathway-supported on all
three architectures and both datasets—the strongest positive
evidence that QRS-morphology encoding is robustly learned
and transferable.
Evidence-limited indicates positive internal evidence whose
external confirmatory evidence is not yet sufficient for a
confident conclusion. ResNet-SBRAD falls here: internal ASS
is positive with CI>0, but external ASS, while directionally
consistent, yields a CI that crosses zero. This designation flags
candidates for further investigation rather than treating them
as failures.
Not-supported subsumes at least four distinct mechanisms
that a negative ASS alone does not distinguish. Disentangling
them is necessary for interpreting what the audit reveals about
model behavior and for guiding next steps.
Type 1—target-sensitive but not target-specific. This is the
pattern observed for 1AVB. PR-window perturbation produces
a substantial performance drop (∆AUROC=−0.226), but the
matched QRS control is even more disruptive (−0.351). The
target pathway is not irrelevant—the model demonstrably
responds to PR-region information—but this dependence does
not exceed a plausible anatomical alternative. Several mech￾anisms could produce this pattern: the model may exploitIEEE JOURNAL OF BIOMEDICAL AND HEALTH INFORMATICS, VOL. XX, NO. XX, MONTH 2025 12
co-occurring QRS or ventricular conduction morphology that
covaries with PR prolongation in the training population; it
may have learned a clinically meaningful proxy not captured
by the pre-specified PR window; or both datasets may share an
acquisition or label artifact that associates PR-interval features
with the label. Critically, Not-supported under this type does
not distinguish an invalid shortcut from a clinically meaningful
but non-pre-specified proxy.

designations are not biological but methodological. Under
zero-masking, AFIB had appeared Pathway-supported (pos￾itive cross-dataset ASS) and CRBBB had appeared transfer￾unstable (negative external ASS). Both patterns reversed under
the primary linear-interpolation operator. These verdicts reflect
perturbation operator artifacts rather than model properties, un￾derscoring the necessity of operator comparison as a standard
audit component.
These subtypes are not mutually exclusive: a single Not￾supported verdict may reflect a combination of low target sen￾sitivity and concurrent reliance on a stronger matched control,
for instance. The taxonomy is a diagnostic tool for interpreting
negative ASS results, not a rigid classification. In this study,
8 of 15 model-disease pairs are Not-supported: 1AVB reflects
Type 1, AFIB reflects Type 2, SBRAD on SE-ResNet and
Transformer reflects Type 3, and the operator-induced Type 4
is prevented by the predefined operator comparison.
F. Relationship to Prior Work
Most prior ECG explanation studies use saliency maps or
single-region perturbation to show that specific signal regions
influence predictions [6], [7], [15]. The present study differs
in two respects. First, we require target-region perturbations
to be compared against matched controls—a stricter criterion
that operationalizes the distinction between sensitivity and
specificity. Second, we evaluate whether evidence-use conclu￾sions persist under frozen-weight transfer to an independent
dataset, addressing the concern that explanation conclusions
may be dataset-specific [4], [10]. The audit protocol is thus an
explanation evaluation method, not an explanation generation
method.
G. Interpretation Boundaries
To clarify what the current audit design can and cannot
support, we distinguish four levels of evidence:
1) Pathway sensitivity: Perturbation of the target evidence
unit causes a performance drop.
2) Pathway specificity: The target-evidence-unit drop ex￾ceeds the drop from matched control perturbations
(ASS>0).
3) Mechanistic validity: The model uses the same physi￾ological mechanisms that clinicians employ.
4) Clinical validity: The mechanism holds under physician
annotation or predicts real clinical outcomes.
The audit conclusions in this paper are structured around
pathway sensitivity and specificity (levels 1–2). Claims about
mechanistic or clinical validity (levels 3–4) require additional
evidence—clinician review of failure cases, formal mediation
analysis, or prospective validation—beyond the scope of this
study. Pathway-supported designations indicate that a model’s
predictions are more sensitive to disease-relevant than to
control-region perturbation under a primary operator; they do
not certify mechanistic or clinical validity.
H. Limitations
We acknowledge the following limitations, organized by
their implications for the audit framework:
1) Single-domain validation: The framework is validated
only in 12-lead ECG classification. Extension to imag￾ing, pathology, text, or multimodal diagnosis requires
domain-specific definitions of evidence units, matched
controls, and perturbation operators. The present study
demonstrates the audit principle in one domain; cross￾domain validation remains future work.
2) Dependence on pre-specifiable evidence units: The
framework requires that domain knowledge can define
target evidence units and plausible matched controls a
priori. It is not applicable to tasks where evidence units

8) No proof of causal mechanism: The audit evaluates

9) Limited to 5 conditions: Extension to additional diag￾noses, subgroup and fairness analyses, and cardiologist

H. Future Work
Several directions merit further investigation. Cross-domain
validation of the matched-control audit principle in imaging,
pathology, or multimodal diagnosis would test the frame￾work’s generality claim. External replication across addi￾tional datasets (different continents, devices, populations)
would strengthen the transfer-stability evidence. A dedicated
cardiologist-adjudicated subset of CODE-15% would enable
formal label-noise quantification. More realistic perturbation
designs—physiologically motivated simulations rather than
signal removal—could strengthen mechanistic interpretability.
Finally, the operator-comparison findings demonstrate that the
broader perturbation literature would benefit from community
standards on operator selection, preregistration, and minimal
reporting requirements for perturbation-based audit studies.
VI. CONCLUSION
We present a model-agnostic matched-control perturbation
audit framework for evaluating whether deep learning models
rely on evidence that is concordant with domain knowledge,
and whether such evidence use remains stable under cross￾dataset transfer. The framework is instantiated and validated
in 12-lead ECG classification using a five-disease case-study
panel and three raw-signal architectures, with XGBoost base￾lines providing feature-space context.
Three methodological findings emerge from this instan￾tiation. First, discrimination, target sensitivity, and domain￾evidence concordance are distinct evaluation axes: high AU￾ROC does not imply knowledge-aligned evidence use, and
target perturbation alone—without matched controls—can pro￾duce false-positive pathway claims (as demonstrated by 1AVB
across all three architectures and both datasets). Second, QRS￾morphology evidence use is architecture-invariant and dataset￾invariant: CRBBB and CLBBB reach Pathway-supported on
all three architectures under the primary operator (internal
and external ASS positive with CI>0, CDDC=1.0 for all
6 model-disease pairs), confirming that the framework can
identify genuinely stable knowledge-aligned evidence use.
Third, perturbation operator selection is a first-order method￾ological variable: zero-masking creates boundary artifacts that
can reverse pathway conclusions, and the operator-comparison
battery reveals that AFIB’s apparent cross-dataset positive was
operator artifact.
The protocol combines three design elements—matched
controls, operator selection, and external transfer—that each
independently prevent a different class of false-positive con￾clusion. Matched controls prevent false-positive pathwayIEEE JOURNAL OF BIOMEDICAL AND HEALTH INFORMATICS, VOL. XX, NO. XX, MONTH 2025 13
claims when target sensitivity is high but non-target depen￾dence is higher (1AVB). Operator selection prevents both
false-positive (AFIB) and false-negative (CRBBB) conclusions
introduced by perturbation artifacts.

Fig. 1
summarizes the workflow instantiated in 12-lead ECG clas￾sification:
1) Domain-knowledge-defined evidence panel: For each
diagnosis, target evidence units and matched controls
are pre-specified from established domain knowledge.
In our ECG instantiation, five diagnoses covering three
structurally distinct evidence forms—interval-localized
timing (1AVB), QRS morphology (CRBBB, CLBBB),
and distributed rate/rhythm (SBRAD, AFIB)—serve as
a case-study panel (Section III-C).
2) Matched-control perturbation: The same perturbation
operator is applied to both the target evidence unit
and each matched control. An evidence-use claim re￾quires the target perturbation to be more disruptive than
its strongest matched control. Perturbation classes are
matched to evidence-unit structure: local windows for
temporally localized features, global transformations for
distributed statistical properties (Section III-D).
3) Audit metrics and evidence tiers: The Anatomical
Specificity Score (ASS) quantifies whether the target
perturbation dominates all matched controls. Per-model
evidence tiers constrain what can be claimed under the
primary operator (Section III-E).
4) External transfer testing: Frozen-weight transfer to an
independent dataset tests whether evidence-use conclu￾sions survive dataset shift (Section III-B).
The framework is model-agnostic: the same evidence units,
matched-control comparisons, and evaluation metrics apply to
any classifier accepting the same input modality. We demon￾strate this across three raw-signal architectures (Section III-F),
with XGBoost feature-space baselines providing contextual
representation-level evidence. The five diagnoses are a case￾study panel covering three structurally distinct evidence forms,
not an exhaustive clinical survey.
B. Datasets and External Validation Setting
Internal cohort — CODE-15%. Brazilian 12-lead ECG
dataset: 345,779 exams (400Hz, 10 s) from 233,770 patients
[22]. Labels were derived from an automated ECG interpre￾tation system. Patient-level split: 60% train (207,232), 20%
validation (69,045), 20% test (69,520), random seed 42.IEEE JOURNAL OF BIOMEDICAL AND HEALTH INFORMATICS, VOL. XX, NO. XX, MONTH 2025 4
Label circularity risk. Because CODE-15% labels are au￾tomated rather than physician-adjudicated, models trained on
them may learn to replicate the automated labeling logic
instead of physician-level diagnostic mechanisms. The circu￾larity risk is highest for 1AVB and SBRAD, where automated
rules closely mirror the target features (PR>200 ms and HR￾based thresholds, respectively), moderate for CRBBB/CLBBB
and AFIB, where QRS morphology and atrial activity criteria
are less directly encoded. Internal CODE findings should
therefore be interpreted as evidence about model behavior
relative to the automated-label system. External validation on
cardiologist-validated labels provides the primary credibility
buffer.
External cohort — PTB-XL. German 12-lead ECG
dataset: 21,837 records from 18,885 patients at 500 Hz [21].
We use official patient-level folds: folds 1–8 for reference, fold
9 (n = 2, 183) for threshold retuning, and fold 10 (n = 2, 198)
for testing. Fold 10 labels were validated by cardiologists
and serve as the primary external credibility set.

V. DISCUSSION
A. Discrimination, Target Sensitivity, and Evidence-Use
Alignment Are Distinct Evaluation Axes
The central finding of this study is that discrimination, target
sensitivity, and evidence-use alignment are three distinct eval￾uation axes that cannot substitute for one another. All five dis￾eases achieved AUROC>0.98 on ResNet, and frozen-weight
transfer preserved AUROC>0.93 for all diseases on ResNet
(Table V). Yet the matched-control audit revealed that only
6 of 15 model-disease pairs reach Pathway-supported, with
8 Not supported and 1 Evidence-limited. A discrimination￾only evaluation would have classified all models as successful;
the matched-control audit reveals heterogeneity invisible to
standard benchmarks.
Conversely, a model need not achieve the highest discrim￾ination to provide informative evidence-use behavior. The
Transformer underperforms ResNet on overall discrimination
(Micro-F1 0.6045 vs. 0.7359) but preserves BBB detection
with near-identical F1—and its architecture-specific rhythm
weakness is itself informative about what the architecture
learns. The protocol thus evaluates models along an axis
orthogonal to discrimination.

D. Operator Selection Determines Audit Conclusions
The predefined operator-comparison battery demonstrates
that perturbation operator choice can determine audit conclu￾sions. The same model-disease pair can yield opposite verdicts
under different operators (Section V-E, Type 4), establishing
operator comparison as a methodological requirement rather
than a sensitivity check.
This finding has direct implications for the broader
perturbation-audit literature. Zero-masking remains the most
common occlusion method in ECG and medical imaging per￾turbation studies, yet our results show it can reverse specificity
conclusions. We recommend that future perturbation-based
audit studies: (1) compare at least two operators with different
artifact profiles; (2) prespecify the primary operator before
seeing results; and (3) report operator-comparison results
alongside primary-operator conclusions. Linear interpolation
is not claimed to be universally optimal, but its continuity￾preserving property eliminates a known artifact class that zero￾masking introduces.
E. Interpreting Audit Verdicts: Why Pathways Are Supported,
Limited, or Not Supported
The audit assigns each (architecture, disease) pair to one
of three evidence tiers. These verdicts do not map directly to
judgments of model correctness or clinical reasoning ability.
We interpret each tier’s meaning and, for Not-supported ver￾dicts, disentangle the distinct mechanisms that can produce a
negative ASS.
Pathway-supported indicates that, under the pre-specified
target and control windows, the primary perturbation op￾erator, and external transfer validation, the target evidence
unit dominates all matched anatomical controls. It does not
certify that the model “reasons like a clinician” or that the
mechanism is physiologically causal (Section V-G). In this
study, CRBBB and CLBBB achieve Pathway-supported on all
three architectures and both datasets—the strongest positive
evidence that QRS-morphology encoding is robustly learned
and transferable.
Evidence-limited indicates positive internal evidence whose
external confirmatory evidence is not yet sufficient for a
confident conclusion. ResNet-SBRAD falls here: internal ASS
is positive with CI>0, but external ASS, while directionally
consistent, yields a CI that crosses zero. This designation flags
candidates for further investigation rather than treating them
as failures.
Not-supported subsumes at least four distinct mechanisms
that a negative ASS alone does not distinguish. Disentangling
them is necessary for interpreting what the audit reveals about
model behavior and for guiding next steps.
Type 1—target-sensitive but not target-specific. This is the
pattern observed for 1AVB. PR-window perturbation produces
a substantial performance drop (∆AUROC=−0.226), but the
matched QRS control is even more disruptive (−0.351). The
target pathway is not irrelevant—the model demonstrably
responds to PR-region information—but this dependence does
not exceed a plausible anatomical alternative. Several mech￾anisms could produce this pattern: the model may exploitIEEE JOURNAL OF BIOMEDICAL AND HEALTH INFORMATICS, VOL. XX, NO. XX, MONTH 2025 12
co-occurring QRS or ventricular conduction morphology that
covaries with PR prolongation in the training population; it
may have learned a clinically meaningful proxy not captured
by the pre-specified PR window; or both datasets may share an
acquisition or label artifact that associates PR-interval features
with the label. Critically, Not-supported under this type does
not distinguish an invalid shortcut from a clinically meaningful
but non-pre-specified proxy.

Type 4—operator-induced verdict. Some Not-supported
designations are not biological but methodological. Under
zero-masking, AFIB had appeared Pathway-supported (pos￾itive cross-dataset ASS) and CRBBB had appeared transfer￾unstable (negative external ASS). Both patterns reversed under
the primary linear-interpolation operator. These verdicts reflect
perturbation operator artifacts rather than model properties, un￾derscoring the necessity of operator comparison as a standard
audit component.
These subtypes are not mutually exclusive: a single Not￾supported verdict may reflect a combination of low target sen￾sitivity and concurrent reliance on a stronger matched control,
for instance. The taxonomy is a diagnostic tool for interpreting
negative ASS results, not a rigid classification. In this study,
8 of 15 model-disease pairs are Not-supported: 1AVB reflects
Type 1, AFIB reflects Type 2, SBRAD on SE-ResNet and
Transformer reflects Type 3, and the operator-induced Type 4
is prevented by the predefined operator comparison.
F. Relationship to Prior Work
Most prior ECG explanation studies use saliency maps or
single-region perturbation to show that specific signal regions
influence predictions [6], [7], [15]. The present study differs
in two respects. First, we require target-region perturbations
to be compared against matched controls—a stricter criterion
that operationalizes the distinction between sensitivity and
specificity. Second, we evaluate whether evidence-use conclu￾sions persist under frozen-weight transfer to an independent
dataset, addressing the concern that explanation conclusions
may be dataset-specific [4], [10]. The audit protocol is thus an
explanation evaluation method, not an explanation generation
method.
G. Interpretation Boundaries
To clarify what the current audit design can and cannot
support, we distinguish four levels of evidence:
1) Pathway sensitivity: Perturbation of the target evidence
unit causes a performance drop.
2) Pathway specificity: The target-evidence-unit drop ex￾ceeds the drop from matched control perturbations
(ASS>0).
3) Mechanistic validity: The model uses the same physi￾ological mechanisms that clinicians employ.
4) Clinical validity: The mechanism holds under physician
annotation or predicts real clinical outcomes.
The audit conclusions in this paper are structured around
pathway sensitivity and specificity (levels 1–2). Claims about
mechanistic or clinical validity (levels 3–4) require additional
evidence—clinician review of failure cases, formal mediation
analysis, or prospective validation—beyond the scope of this
study. Pathway-supported designations indicate that a model’s
predictions are more sensitive to disease-relevant than to
control-region perturbation under a primary operator; they do
not certify mechanistic or clinical validity.
H. Limitations
We acknowledge the following limitations, organized by
their implications for the audit framework:
1) Single-domain validation: The framework is validated
only in 12-lead ECG classification. Extension to imag￾ing, pathology, text, or multimodal diagnosis requires
domain-specific definitions of evidence units, matched
controls, and perturbation operators. The present study
demonstrates the audit principle in one domain; cross￾domain validation remains future work.
2) Dependence on pre-specifiable evidence units: The
framework requires that domain knowledge can define
target evidence units and plausible matched controls a
priori. It is not applicable to tasks where evidence units
cannot be localized or where domain consensus on what
constitutes a relevant evidence unit is absent.IEEE JOURNAL OF BIOMEDICAL AND HEALTH INFORMATICS, VOL. XX, NO.

We present a model-agnostic matched-control perturbation
audit framework for evaluating whether deep learning models
rely on evidence that is concordant with domain knowledge,
and whether such evidence use remains stable under cross￾dataset transfer. The framework is instantiated and validated

B. Matched Controls Are a Necessary Safeguard
The 1AVB case establishes that matched controls are a nec￾essary safeguard against false-positive evidence-use claims. A
target-only perturbation study would have reported a positive
finding (∆AUROC=−0.226), but matched QRS perturbation
is more disruptive (−0.351), yielding negative ASS across all

mechanisms behind this pattern). Any explanation method that
tests only whether a target region matters, without comparing
against plausible matched controls, is vulnerable to the same
class of false-positive conclusion—a principle that generalizes
beyond ECG to any domain where evidence units can be
specified a priori.
C. External Transfer Separates Stable from Unstable Evidence
Use
Treating frozen-weight external transfer as a stress test of
evidence use reveals that evidence-use conclusions can be
dataset-specific. CRBBB and CLBBB survive this test on all
three architectures under the primary operator (CDDC=1.0 for
all 6 pairs), providing the framework’s strongest positive evi￾dence: QRS-morphology evidence use is architecture-invariant

zero-masking positive as operator artifact—ASS is negative on
both datasets under the primary operator.

D. Operator Selection Determines Audit Conclusions
The predefined operator-comparison battery demonstrates
that perturbation operator choice can determine audit conclu￾sions. The same model-disease pair can yield opposite verdicts
under different operators (Section V-E, Type 4), establishing
operator comparison as a methodological requirement rather
than a sensitivity check.
This finding has direct implications for the broader
perturbation-audit literature. Zero-masking remains the most
common occlusion method in ECG and medical imaging per￾turbation studies, yet our results show it can reverse specificity
conclusions. We recommend that future perturbation-based
audit studies: (1) compare at least two operators with different
artifact profiles; (2) prespecify the primary operator before
seeing results; and (3) report operator-comparison results
alongside primary-operator conclusions. Linear interpolation
is not claimed to be universally optimal, but its continuity￾preserving property eliminates a known artifact class that zero￾masking introduces.
E. Interpreting Audit Verdicts: Why Pathways Are Supported,
Limited, or Not Supported
The audit assigns each (architecture, disease) pair to one
of three evidence tiers. These verdicts do not map directly to
judgments of model correctness or clinical reasoning ability.
We interpret each tier’s meaning and, for Not-supported ver￾dicts, disentangle the distinct mechanisms that can produce a
negative ASS.
Pathway-supported indicates that, under the pre-specified
target and control windows, the primary perturbation op￾erator, and external transfer validation, the target evidence
unit dominates all matched anatomical controls. It does not
certify that the model “reasons like a clinician” or that the
mechanism is physiologically causal (Section V-G). In this
study, CRBBB and CLBBB achieve Pathway-supported on all
three architectures and both datasets—the strongest positive
evidence that QRS-morphology encoding is robustly learned
and transferable.
Evidence-limited indicates positive internal evidence whose
external confirmatory evidence is not yet sufficient for a
confident conclusion. ResNet-SBRAD falls here: internal ASS
is positive with CI>0, but external ASS, while directionally
consistent, yields a CI that crosses zero. This designation flags
candidates for further investigation rather than treating them
as failures.
Not-supported subsumes at least four distinct mechanisms
that a negative ASS alone does not distinguish. Disentangling
them is necessary for interpreting what the audit reveals about
model behavior and for guiding next steps.
Type 1—target-sensitive but not target-specific. This is the
pattern observed for 1AVB. PR-window perturbation produces
a substantial performance drop (∆AUROC=−0.226), but the
matched QRS control is even more disruptive (−0.351). The
target pathway is not irrelevant—the model demonstrably
responds to PR-region information—but this dependence does
not exceed a plausible anatomical alternative. Several mech￾anisms could produce this pattern: the model may exploitIEEE JOURNAL OF BIOMEDICAL AND HEALTH INFORMATICS, VOL. XX, NO. XX, MONTH 2025 12
co-occurring QRS or ventricular conduction morphology that
covaries with PR prolongation in the training population; it
may have learned a clinically meaningful proxy not captured
by the pre-specified PR window; or both datasets may share an
acquisition or label artifact that associates PR-interval features
with the label. Critically, Not-supported under this type does
not distinguish an invalid shortcut from a clinically meaningful
but non-pre-specified proxy.

D. Operator Selection Determines Audit Conclusions
The predefined operator-comparison battery demonstrates
that perturbation operator choice can reverse evidence-use
conclusions. Zero-masking creates hard-boundary artifacts
that systematically inflate control-region disruption, produc￾ing both false-positive (AFIB) and false-negative (CRBBB)
evidence-use conclusions depending on how the artifact inter￾acts with the specific waveform structures being perturbed.
This finding has direct implications for the broader
perturbation-audit literature. Zero-masking remains the most
common occlusion method in ECG and medical imaging per￾turbation studies, yet our results show it can reverse specificity
conclusions. We recommend that future perturbation-based
audit studies: (1) compare at least two operators with different
artifact profiles; (2) prespecify the primary operator before
seeing results; and (3) report operator-comparison results
alongside primary-operator conclusions. Linear interpolation
is not claimed to be universally optimal, but its continuity￾preserving property eliminates a known artifact class that zero￾masking introduces.
E. Relationship to Prior Work
Most prior ECG explanation studies use saliency maps or
single-region perturbation to show that specific signal regions
influence predictions [6], [7], [15]. The present study differs
in two respects. First, we require target-region perturbations
to be compared against matched controls—a stricter criterion
that operationalizes the distinction between sensitivity and
specificity. Second, we evaluate whether evidence-use conclu￾sions persist under frozen-weight transfer to an independent
dataset, addressing the concern that explanation conclusions
may be dataset-specific [4], [10]. The audit protocol is thus an
explanation evaluation method, not an explanation generation
method.
F. Interpretation Boundaries
To clarify what the current audit design can and cannot
support, we distinguish four levels of evidence:
1) Pathway sensitivity: Perturbation of the target evidence
unit causes a performance drop.
2) Pathway specificity: The target-evidence-unit drop ex￾ceeds the drop from matched control perturbations
(ASS>0).
3) Mechanistic validity: The model uses the same physi￾ological mechanisms that clinicians employ.
4) Clinical validity: The mechanism holds under physician
annotation or predicts real clinical outcomes.
The audit conclusions in this paper are structured around
pathway sensitivity and specificity (levels 1–2). Claims aboutIEEE JOURNAL OF BIOMEDICAL AND HEALTH INFORMATICS, VOL. XX, NO. XX, MONTH 2025 12
mechanistic or clinical validity (levels 3–4) require additional
evidence—clinician review of failure cases, formal mediation
analysis, or prospective validation—beyond the scope of this
study. Pathway-supported designations indicate that a model’s
predictions are more sensitive to disease-relevant than to
control-region perturbation under a primary operator; they do
not certify mechanistic or clinical validity.
G. Limitations
We acknowledge the following limitations, organized by
their implications for the audit framework:
1) Single-domain validation: The framework is validated
only in 12-lead ECG classification.

audit framework for evaluating whether deep learning models
rely on evidence that is concordant with domain knowledge,
and whether such evidence use remains stable under cross￾dataset transfer. The framework is instantiated and validated
in 12-lead ECG classification using a five-disease case-study
panel and three raw-signal architectures, with XGBoost base￾lines providing feature-space context.
Three methodological findings emerge from this instan￾tiation. First, discrimination, target sensitivity, and domain￾evidence concordance are distinct evaluation axes: high AU￾ROC does not imply knowledge-aligned evidence use, and
target perturbation alone—without matched controls—can pro￾duce false-positive pathway claims (as demonstrated by 1AVB
across all three architectures and both datasets). Second, QRS￾morphology evidence use is architecture-invariant and dataset￾invariant: CRBBB and CLBBB reach Pathway-supported on
all three architectures under the primary operator (internal
and external ASS positive with CI>0, CDDC=1.0 for all
6 model-disease pairs), confirming that the framework can
identify genuinely stable knowledge-aligned evidence use.
Third, perturbation operator selection is a first-order method￾ological variable: zero-masking creates boundary artifacts that
can reverse pathway conclusions, and the operator-comparison
battery reveals that AFIB’s apparent cross-dataset positive was
operator artifact.
The protocol combines three design elements—matched
controls, operator selection, and external transfer—that each
independently prevent a different class of false-positive con￾clusion. Matched controls prevent false-positive pathwayIEEE JOURNAL OF BIOMEDICAL AND HEALTH INFORMATICS, VOL. XX, NO. XX, MONTH 2025 13
claims when target sensitivity is high but non-target depen￾dence is higher (1AVB). Operator selection prevents both
false-positive (AFIB) and false-negative (CRBBB) conclusions
introduced by perturbation artifacts.

Despite these advances, three structural limitations persist.
First, existing perturbation studies rarely incorporate matched
anatomical controls: they test whether a region matters, but
not whether disease-specific regions matter more than adjacent
control regions. This is the distinction between sensitivity and
specificity in explanation evaluation. Second, the perturbation
operator is rarely treated as an auditable variable—zero￾masking is the default, and its artifacts are seldom quantified.
Third, explanation conclusions are typically validated only
within the training distribution; Adebayo et al. [8] showed
that saliency maps can fail basic sanity checks under input
transformations, but the broader question of whether explana￾tion claims survive dataset shift remains underexamined [4],
[9].
C. Cross-Dataset Transfer and Generalization
The two largest public 12-lead ECG datasets—PTB-XL [21]
(21,837 records, cardiologist-validated labels) and CODE-15%
[22] (345,779 exams, automated labels)—differ fundamentally
in their label sources. This asymmetry creates a natural testbed
for transfer stability: models trained on automated labels may
learn to replicate the labeling logic rather than physician-level
diagnostic features. Cross-dataset validation remains underuti￾lized in ECG deep learning. Soltanieh et al. [23] addressed
out-of-distribution generalization for self-supervised ECG rep￾resentations. Frank et al. [24] reported substantial performance
drops for myocardial ischemia detection across six public ECG
databases. At foundation-model scale, ECGFounder [25] and
recent benchmarking efforts [26] confirm that cross-domain
generalization remains challenging even for large pre-trained
models.
The consistent picture is that external validation is widely
recommended but rarely executed, and even less often applied
to explanation claims. Our study addresses this gap by treat￾ing frozen-weight transfer from CODE-15% to cardiologist￾validated PTB-XL fold 10 as a simultaneous check on both
prediction quality and evidence-use stability.
D. Clinical ECG Knowledge and Model Auditing
Clinical ECG interpretation relies on well-defined phys￾iological features: PR interval for AV conduction timing,
QRS duration and morphology for ventricular conduction,
RR interval regularity for rhythm classification, and P-wave
morphology for atrial activity [11]. These features define
distinct, auditable evidence units with well-characterized sig￾nal structure. Recent studies have tested whether deep ECG
models learn clinically meaningful features: Hempel et al. [27]
reported that 96.0% of high-confidence 1AVB predictions had
PR>200ms; Riberg et al. [28] found that RR interval fea￾tures dominated for bradycardia while morphological features
showed weaker correlation; Hammer et al. [29] introduced an
architecture separating rhythm and morphology processing. A
systematic review by Ayano et al. [30] confirmed increasing
focus on clinical parameters.
However, existing studies confirm that models attend to
clinically relevant features but do not test whether disease￾specific signal regions dominate over anatomically adjacent
controls, or whether such pathway specificity survives dataset
shift. Demonstrating feature relevance is not the same as
demonstrating feature specificity. Our framework addresses
this gap by transforming clinical pathway knowledge into
testable, falsifiable audit criteria with matched controls and
external transfer.
III. METHODS
A. Audit Framework Overview
The audit framework has four general components: domain￾defined target evidence units, matched controls, operator￾specified perturbation, and external transfer testing.

audits provide incomplete evidence.

The predefined operator-comparison battery demonstrates
that perturbation operator choice can determine audit conclu￾sions. The same model-disease pair can yield opposite verdicts
under different operators (Section V-E, Type 4), establishing
operator comparison as a methodological requirement rather
than a sensitivity check.

perturbation-audit literature. Zero-masking remains the most
common occlusion method in ECG and medical imaging per￾turbation studies, yet our results show it can reverse specificity
conclusions. We recommend that future perturbation-based
audit studies: (1) compare at least two operators with different
artifact profiles; (2) prespecify the primary operator before
seeing results; and (3) report operator-comparison results
alongside primary-operator conclusions. Linear interpolation
is not claimed to be universally optimal, but its continuity￾preserving property eliminates a known artifact class that zero￾masking introduces.
E. Interpreting Audit Verdicts: Why Pathways Are Supported,
Limited, or Not Supported
The audit assigns each (architecture, disease) pair to one
of three evidence tiers. These verdicts do not map directly to

We interpret each tier’s meaning and, for Not-supported ver￾dicts, disentangle the distinct mechanisms that can produce a

Figure 4 summarises the complete per-model audit results
under the primary linear-interpolation operator; full statistics

on all three architectures), 1/15 as Evidence-limited (SBRAD￾ResNet), and 8/15 as Not supported (1AVB and AFIB on all
three architectures; SBRAD on SE-ResNet and Transformer).

evidence.

XGBoost Clinical-MVP Features (110D):
• Block 1—Signal Quality (2 features): Signal-to￾noise ratio (SNR dB) and baseline wander index (low￾frequency power ratio), computed from lead II.
• Block 2—Rhythm & Rate (15 features): Beat count,
heart rate statistics (mean, std, min, max), RR interval
statistics (mean, std, min, max, median, range), and
RR variability metrics (RMSSD, SDNN, CV, pNN50,
RR irregularity index). Computed from R-peak positions
detected via NeuroKit2’s Elgendi algorithm [36].
• Block 3—AV Conduction Timing (6 features): PR￾proxy interval statistics (median, mean, std, min, max)
and P-wave detectability. P-waves detected as the maxi￾mum amplitude point in an 80–200ms window preceding
each R-peak (Lead II), with the PR-proxy computed as
the temporal distance from P-wave peak to subsequent R￾peak. Physiological constraints (PR-proxy ∈ [80, 400]ms,
P-wave ∈ [60, 140]ms) applied to filter implausible de￾tections.
• Block 4—QRS Morphology & Conduction (15 fea￾tures): QRS duration statistics (mean, std, min, max),
QRS frontal axis computed from net deflection in leads
I and aVF [11], R/S amplitude ratio statistics, terminal
S-wave amplitude, and additional morphological descrip￾tors.
• Per-lead amplitude statistics (72 features: mean, std,
min, max, range, RMS for 12 leads). Total: 2 signal
quality + 15 rhythm + 6 AV timing + 15 QRS morphology
+ 72 amplitude = 110 dimensions.
Implementation used NeuroKit2 [36] for R-peak detection
(∼2ms/sample) and custom SciPy signal processing for P￾wave detection, QRS duration estimation, QRS axis compu￾tation, and R/S ratio calculation. The pipeline provides prag￾matic proxy measurements, not clinical fiducial annotation.
Processed all 345,779 exams in approximately 2 hours (∼50
samples/second).
C. Model Architecture Details
1D ResNet (1.2M parameters):
• Input: Raw 12-lead ECG (12 × 4096), z-score normal￾ized per lead
• Preprocessing: Original signals (4000 samples at 400Hz,
10s duration) resampled to 4096 samples via linear inter￾polation (10.24s), providing power-of-two input length
for 4× downsampling stages
• Backbone: 4 ResNet stages—Stage 1: 2 blocks, 64
channels, kernel=7, stride=2; Stage 2: 2 blocks, 128
channels, kernel=7, stride=2; Stage 3: 2 blocks, 256
channels, kernel=7, stride=2; Stage 4: 2 blocks, 512
channels, kernel=7, stride=2
• Residual block: Conv1D → BatchNorm → ReLU →
Conv1D → BatchNorm → skip connection → ReLU
• Pooling: AdaptiveAvgPool1D(1) → flatten to 512-dim
vector
• Classifier: Dropout(0.2) → Linear(512 → 5) → Sigmoid
• Loss: BCEWithLogitsLoss with per-class weights (in￾verse prevalence)

D. Operator Selection Determines Audit Conclusions
The predefined operator-comparison battery demonstrates
that perturbation operator choice can determine audit conclu￾sions. The same model-disease pair can yield opposite verdicts
under different operators (Section V-E, Type 4), establishing
operator comparison as a methodological requirement rather
than a sensitivity check.
This finding has direct implications for the broader
perturbation-audit literature. Zero-masking remains the most
common occlusion method in ECG and medical imaging per￾turbation studies, yet our results show it can reverse specificity
conclusions. We recommend that future perturbation-based
audit studies: (1) compare at least two operators with different
artifact profiles; (2) prespecify the primary operator before
seeing results; and (3) report operator-comparison results
alongside primary-operator conclusions. Linear interpolation
is not claimed to be universally optimal, but its continuity￾preserving property eliminates a known artifact class that zero￾masking introduces.
E. Interpreting Audit Verdicts: Why Pathways Are Supported,
Limited, or Not Supported
The audit assigns each (architecture, disease) pair to one
of three evidence tiers. These verdicts do not map directly to
judgments of model correctness or clinical reasoning ability.
We interpret each tier’s meaning and, for Not-supported ver￾dicts, disentangle the distinct mechanisms that can produce a
negative ASS.
Pathway-supported indicates that, under the pre-specified
target and control windows, the primary perturbation op￾erator, and external transfer validation, the target evidence
unit dominates all matched anatomical controls. It does not
certify that the model “reasons like a clinician” or that the
mechanism is physiologically causal (Section V-G). In this
study, CRBBB and CLBBB achieve Pathway-supported on all
three architectures and both datasets—the strongest positive
evidence that QRS-morphology encoding is robustly learned
and transferable.
Evidence-limited indicates positive internal evidence whose
external confirmatory evidence is not yet sufficient for a
confident conclusion. ResNet-SBRAD falls here: internal ASS
is positive with CI>0, but external ASS, while directionally
consistent, yields a CI that crosses zero. This designation flags
candidates for further investigation rather than treating them
as failures.
Not-supported subsumes at least four distinct mechanisms
that a negative ASS alone does not distinguish. Disentangling
them is necessary for interpreting what the audit reveals about
model behavior and for guiding next steps.
Type 1—target-sensitive but not target-specific. This is the
pattern observed for 1AVB. PR-window perturbation produces
a substantial performance drop (∆AUROC=−0.226), but the
matched QRS control is even more disruptive (−0.351). The
target pathway is not irrelevant—the model demonstrably
responds to PR-region information—but this dependence does
not exceed a plausible anatomical alternative. Several mech￾anisms could produce this pattern: the model may exploitIEEE JOURNAL OF BIOMEDICAL AND HEALTH INFORMATICS, VOL. XX, NO. XX, MONTH 2025 12
co-occurring QRS or ventricular conduction morphology that
covaries with PR prolongation in the training population; it
may have learned a clinically meaningful proxy not captured
by the pre-specified PR window; or both datasets may share an
acquisition or label artifact that associates PR-interval features
with the label. Critically, Not-supported under this type does
not distinguish an invalid shortcut from a clinically meaningful
but non-pre-specified proxy.

我觉得**现在已经基本 OK，而且比上一版明显完整很多**。你之前担心的核心问题——“三种 audit verdict 背后到底意味着什么”——现在 Discussion E 已经补上了：它先解释 Pathway-supported / Evidence-limited / Not-supported 的含义，然后把 Not-supported 拆成 Type 1 target-sensitive but not target-specific、Type 2 low target sensitivity、Type 3 architecture/dataset-contingent、Type 4 operator-induced verdict。这个结构是对的，也确实让方法论从“给结论”变成了“诊断证据使用模式”。fileciteturn7file1 fileciteturn7file2

我建议再做 **3 个小调整**，不然现在有点“内容对了，但表达还可以更稳”。

**第一，建议把 Section E 提前。**  
现在顺序是 A 总论 → B matched controls → C external transfer → D operator → E verdict interpretation。逻辑也能通，但读者最关心的其实就是 E。你可以改成：

A. Discrimination, Target Sensitivity, and Evidence-Use Alignment Are Distinct Evaluation Axes  
B. Interpreting Audit Verdicts: Why Pathways Are Supported, Limited, or Not Supported  
C. Matched Controls Are a Necessary Safeguard  
D. External Transfer Separates Stable from Unstable Evidence Use  
E. Operator Selection Determines Audit Conclusions  
F. Relationship to Prior Work  
G. Interpretation Boundaries  
H. Limitations

这样 Discussion 的主轴更像：**先解释发现，再抽象方法论意义**。现在的 B/C/D 有点像又把 Results 总结了一遍，E 反而被放到后面，重点稍微被埋了。

**第二，Type 4 的说法要稍微改一下。**  
现在写的是 “Not-supported subsumes at least four distinct mechanisms”，然后 Type 4 是 operator-induced verdict。但严格说，Type 4 不是一个“negative ASS 本身的生物学/模型机制”，而是一个**审计方法导致 verdict 改变的机制**。尤其你们现在最终 tier 是在 primary linear interpolation 下定的，operator-induced 其实是被 operator comparison 防住的错误，而不是当前 Not-supported 的直接原因。建议把这句：

> Not-supported subsumes at least four distinct mechanisms...

改成：

> Not-supported verdicts and apparent verdict disagreements can arise from several distinct sources. Some reflect model evidence use, whereas others reflect the audit operator itself.

然后 Type 4 标题可以改成：

> Type 4—operator-induced apparent verdict.

这样更严谨。你们前面已经说明 zero-masking 会让 AFIB 看起来 Pathway-supported、让 CRBBB 看起来 transfer-unstable，但 primary operator 下这些会反转；这个本质是“apparent verdict artifact”，不是和 1AVB/AFIB/SBRAD 并列的模型证据模式。fileciteturn8file5

**第三，1AVB 那段有一句建议改得更准确。**  
现在 Type 1 里写：

> both datasets may share an acquisition or label artifact that associates PR-interval features with the label.

但这一段的重点是 **QRS control 比 PR target 更强**，所以 shared artifact 如果存在，更可能是把 **QRS-related morphology / acquisition pattern** 和 1AVB label 关联起来，而不是把 PR-interval features 和 label 关联起来。建议改成：

> or both datasets may share an acquisition or label-source artifact that associates QRS-related morphology, recording conditions, or other non-PR proxies with the 1AVB label.

这个更贴合你们的 ASS 结果：PR 有影响，但没有超过 QRS matched control。fileciteturn7file1

其他部分我觉得不错。A 现在能立住总论：高 AUROC 和 evidence alignment 分开；B/C/D 分别对应 matched control、external transfer、operator selection 三个方法论贡献；E 解释 verdict 背后的机制；G 又把 pathway specificity 和 mechanistic/clinical validity 区分开，这个很重要，可以防止审稿人说你们 claim 过度。fileciteturn8file3 fileciteturn7file2

我的判断：**这版可以作为正式 Discussion 的基础了**。再把 E 提前、Type 4 改成 apparent verdict、1AVB artifact 那句修一下，就比较稳。
